newsitem.title: MALDIVES: FEATURE-Low-lying Maldives stand tall against thre.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Low-lying Maldives stand tall against thre.

text.p: Except for the flies, this palm-fringed island could be paradise.
The circle of sand was not here six years ago. But islands come and go in this Indian Ocean archipelago and no one is keeping a precise tally.
"How do you define an island?" Maldivian Environment Minister Abdul Rasheed Hussain asks. "We cannot precisely say how many there are. It is an ongoing process and it's hard to keep track."
As an approximation, the government has settled on 1,190 -- 199 inhabited, the others simply beckoning.

Thilafushi -- "Landfill Island" -- is one of the newcomers, the Maldives' answer to one of the inevitable ills that prosperity spurred by tourism has brought to this equatorial nation which is the size of Portugal but 99.669 percent water.
VEGETABLES ON A GARBAGE DUMP
Every day a vessel named "Ufuli" carrying four trucks crosses from Male to the turquoise lagoon surrounding Thilafushi, docks at a spit of sand and unloads 105 tonnes of garbage.
It began in 1991, when planners realised refuse thrown up by the construction and tourism boom could no longer be incinerated or simply dropped in the ocean without damaging the environment.
"Our seas are not a dumping ground," Hussain said.
They picked a shallow lagoon a 15-minute boat ride to the west of the capital Male and, with daily deposits of garbage and dredging of sand, created a tropical island.
"The flies are here because there was a recent discharge," Simad Saeed, a senior Environment Ministry official, explains as we walk between parallel lines of coconut trees.

There is no odour -- only non-combustible items are shipped to the dump -- and tangled, tropical vegetation has invaded all but one edge of the island where tin cans, plastic bottles and scrap metal lie neatly sorted on the sun-drenched sand.
"Much of the imported material, unlike our indigenous goods, is plastic and not biodegradable," Saeed says. "We have launched a campaign to discourage plastic bags, which suffocate the coral."

Worried that the landfill might be spawning its own set of problems, the Maldives brought in foreign consultants to study whether pollution was seeping into the environment. "They grew vegetables to see if anything bad was coming up through their roots. Amazingly we found no problem," he says.
SURVIVAL OF THE TALLEST
Garbage is hardly the biggest environmental problem facing the Maldives. How about disappearance?
With its highest point only eight feet (2.4 metres) above the enveloping sea, the Maldives is one of the lowest-lying nations -- even a small rise in the world's oceans could spell the end.
"We are environmentally a very delicate place," Hussain said. The average land height in the Maldives is 1.3 metres (four ft, three inches), and 80 percent is below one metre (yard), he notes.

"It is a question of survival now, survival of the islands themselves. We don't know what is going to happen to them," he says, noting scientists studying global warming were worried that seas swollen by the melting ice cap could swamp the Maldives.
"There is a consensus, but how much, when, how soon it will come, over that there is still debate," the minister said.
WHAT WEIGHS THREE TONNES, HAS FOUR LEGS?
For millenia, since the 26 atolls rose up from ocean floor, coral reefs have been nature's defence for the 828-km (511-mile) long archipelago which is 600 km (375 miles) south of India.

It is just out of reach of the cyclones which sweep through the Bay of Bengal. The highest wind speed recorded on Male was 103 km (64 miles) per hour. But its leaders are not complacent. "We cannot afford to have any wave above one metre," Hussain says.

To bolster defences around Male, authorities have piled hundreds of three-tonne, four-legged blocks called Tetrapods, creating a giant cement seawall that dissipates the energy of the waves but allows water to flow through its cracks.

The Maldives and some 30 other island nations including Mauritius, Cuba and Bermuda are pressing for a global convention that would curb pollutants which contribute to the Greenhouse Effect that many believe is raising the seas.
The Maldives and its allies are pushing for a 20 percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions by 2005.
President Bill Clinton will lay out ideas to reduce global warming over the next 50 years when he addresses the U.N. Earth Summit on Thursday, Under Secretary of State Tim Wirth said.
But Wirth said on Tuesday that the United States will not announce its targets and timetables for emissions reductions until late summer or early fall.
European Union ministers have agreed to 15 percent by 2010, but the United States, Japan and Australia oppose the curbs, deputy environment minister Abdullah Majeed said.
WORLD'S FIRST ENVIRONMENTAL REFUGEES?

Hussain scoffs at reports that Maldivian leaders are secretly searching for a deserted corner of the earth where its citizens could settle if their nation met a watery grave. The favourite rumoured destination is the Australian outback.
"We are a very proud nation. We have never thought of a second home. We never think of refugee status," he said.
"We have chosen to live in this very delicate environment. We would still like to live here. We are very happy to be here. We want to keep this country for centuries to come."
